claims.text: Aluminum and titanium are lightweight alloying elements relative to the heavier constituents being replaced.
Increasing aluminum and titanium while reducing heavier elements will significantly reduce the density of a high-entropy alloy.
The proposed compositional change will produce superior, balanced mechanical and thermal properties under demanding conditions.
CoCrFeMnNi is a near-equiatomic conventional high-entropy alloy containing relatively heavy elements.
Conventional refractory high-entropy alloys can contain significant amounts of heavy refractory metals.
The target material is intended for high-temperature and high-stress aerospace, power-generation, or nuclear environments that may also be corrosive or oxidizing.
The proposed alloy will form a medium- to high-entropy solid-solution matrix supplemented by fine-scale coherent precipitates.
A solid-solution matrix with fine precipitates will strengthen the alloy while reducing its overall density.
Increasing aluminum and titanium enhances lattice distortion.
The enhanced lattice distortion caused by the lightweight-element additions provides solid-solution strengthening.
Controlled precipitation of secondary phases maintains ductility and thermal stability.
High-entropy-induced structural stability and precipitation strengthening jointly produce an optimal balance of properties.
The modified alloy will have lower density than heavier conventional high-entropy or refractory alloys.
The modified alloy will maintain or improve yield strength and ductility relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will maintain or improve high-temperature performance relative to the baseline.
Traditional high-entropy or refractory alloys with larger fractions of heavy elements have higher densities and may exhibit ductility and thermal-stability trade-offs.
The claimed benefits occur only within a limited compositional window.
Excessive lightweight-element addition may destabilize the desired phases or cause excessive softening.
The compositional and processing limits needed to balance strength, ductility, and density are not yet established.
